paragraphs.text: On the sixth day of the month of April: commemoration and life of our blessed father and teacher Methodius, Archbishop of Moravia. Lord, bless, Father.

God, who is good and almighty, brought all things, visible and invisible, from nonexistence into existence and adorned them with every kind of beauty. Anyone who reflects on this beauty, considering it little by little, can understand in part and come to know the one who made such wonderful and numerous works.

For through reflection on the greatness and beauty of the works, their maker is [?]. The angels praise him with the thrice-holy hymn, and all of us who hold the true faith glorify him in the Holy Trinity, that is, in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: in three hypostases, which one may call three persons, but in one Godhead.
For before every hour, time, and age, beyond every mind and incorporeal understanding, the Father himself begot the Son, as Wisdom said: “Before all the hills he begets me.”
And in the Gospel, the Word of God himself, having become flesh in the last days for our salvation, said with his most pure lips: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”
From that same Father the Holy Spirit also proceeds, as the Son himself said with his divine voice: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.”
This God completed all creation, as David says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their host by the spirit of his mouth.”
For he spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and they were created.

Before all else he created man, taking dust from the earth and breathing into him a soul from himself with a life-giving breath, together with rational understanding and free will, so that he might bring him into paradise, giving him a commandment as a test, so that if he kept it, he would remain immortal; but if he transgressed it, he would surely die through his own will, and not by God's command.
But when the devil saw man so honored and [?] in the place from which he himself had fallen through his own pride, he caused him to transgress the commandment.
And he drove man out of paradise and condemned him to death.
From then on the enemy began to incite and deceive the human race with many schemes.

But in his great mercy and love, God did not abandon humanity completely. Rather, in every age and time he chose a man and revealed their deeds and struggles to the people, so that everyone, imitating them, might strive toward what is good.
Such was Enosh, who was the first to hope to call upon the name of the Lord.
Then Enoch, having pleased God, was taken away.
Noah was found righteous in his generation and escaped the flood in the ark, so that the earth might again be filled and adorned with God's creatures.
After the division of languages, when everyone had gone astray, Abraham came to know God and was called his friend, and received the promise: “In your offspring all nations will be blessed.”
Isaac was led up the mountain as a sacrifice, foreshadowing Christ.
Jacob destroyed his father-in-law's idols and saw a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, with God's angels ascending it, and in his blessings upon his sons he prophesied about Christ.
Joseph fed the people in Egypt, showing himself to be a man of God.
The books tell of Job of Uz, righteous, truthful, and blameless: he underwent trials and endured them, and was blessed by God.

Moses, together with Aaron among God's priests, was called a god to Pharaoh, afflicted Egypt, and led God's people out, by day with a bright cloud and by night with a pillar of fire. He parted the sea, and they crossed on dry ground, but he drowned the Egyptians, and in the waterless wilderness he gave the people water to drink and fed them their fill of angels' bread and birds. He spoke with God face to face, as far as it is possible for a human being to speak with God, and gave the people the law, written by God's finger.
Joshua son of Nun divided the land among God's people, having waged war against their enemies.
The judges likewise won many victories.
Samuel, having received God's mercy, anointed and appointed a king at the Lord's word.
David shepherded the people with gentleness and taught them songs of God.
Solomon, having received wisdom from God beyond all other people, composed many good teachings in proverbs, although he himself did not persevere to the end.

Elijah exposed the people's wickedness through famine, raised a dead boy, and brought fire down from heaven by his word, burning up many people and consuming the sacrifices with wondrous fire, and, having slain the abominable priests, ascended to heaven in a fiery chariot with horses, giving his disciple a double portion of his spirit.
Elisha received the mantle and performed twice as many miracles.
The other prophets, each in his own time, prophesied about wondrous things that were to happen.
John, the great mediator after these between the old law and the new, was Christ's baptizer, witness, and herald to both the living and the dead.
The holy apostles Peter and Paul, with the other disciples of Christ, passed through the whole world like lightning and enlightened the entire earth.
After them, the martyrs washed away defilement with their own blood, and the successors of the holy apostles, having baptized the emperor, destroyed paganism through many struggles and labors.

Sylvester, honorably receiving the support of the great emperor Constantine together with 318 fathers, convened the first council at Nicaea, defeated Arius, and anathematized him and his heresy, which he raised against the Holy Trinity, just as Abraham once, with three hundred and eighteen young men, defeated the kings and received a blessing, bread, and wine from Melchizedek, king of Salem, for he was a priest of God Most High.

Damasus and Gregory the Theologian, with 150 fathers and the great emperor Theodosius, confirmed the holy Creed at Constantinople, that is, “I believe in one God,” and, cutting Macedonius off, anathematized him and the blasphemy he spoke against the Holy Spirit.
Celestine and Cyril, with 200 fathers and another emperor, overthrew Nestorius at Ephesus, together with all the falsehood he spoke against Christ.
Leo and Anatolius, with the orthodox emperor Marcian and with six [?] hundred and thirty fathers at Chalcedon condemned the madness and error of Eutyches.
Vigilius, together with the God-pleasing Justin and one hundred and sixty-five fathers, convened a council, investigated, and pronounced condemnation.

Agatho, the apostolic pope, together with two hundred and seventy fathers and the honorable Emperor Constantine, uprooted many disturbances at the Sixth Council. They expelled and condemned, together with all their fellow council members, those men—I mean Theodore of Pharan, Sergius and Pyrrhus, Cyrus of Alexandria, Honorius of Rome, Macarius of Antioch, and their other supporters—and established and strengthened the Christian faith in truth.

After all these, the merciful God, who desires every person to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, in our own time, for the sake of our people, for whom no one had ever cared, raised up our teacher, the blessed Methodius, to a worthy office. We need not be ashamed to compare all his good deeds and labors, one by one, with those of these servants of God.
For he was equal to some, a little inferior to others, and greater than still others, surpassing those skilled in speech by his deeds, and those skilled in deeds by his speech.

For, becoming like them all, he displayed the example of them all [?]: fear of God, observance of the commandments, bodily purity, earnest prayers and holiness, speech both forceful and gentle—forceful toward opponents, but gentle toward those who accepted instruction— anger, gentleness, mercy, love, suffering, and endurance, becoming all things to all people so that he might win them all.
His family on both sides was not lowly, but very good and honorable, known first to God, and also to the emperor and the whole region of Thessalonica, as his bodily appearance itself showed.

For this reason the dignitaries, loving him from childhood, treated him with honor in their conversations, until the emperor, his quick intelligence [?], gave him a Slavic principality to govern—as I would say, foreseeing that he intended to send him to the Slavs as a teacher and their first archbishop— so that he might learn all the Slavic customs and gradually become accustomed to them.
After spending many years in that principality and seeing the many disorderly disturbances of this life, he turned his will from earthly darkness to heavenly thoughts.
For he did not wish to trouble his honorable soul with things that do not endure forever.

Finding an opportunity, he freed himself from his rule and went to Olympus, where the holy fathers live. He received the tonsure, put on black robes, and lived in humble obedience, fulfilling the entire monastic rule and devoting himself to books.
When such an occasion arose, the emperor sent for his brother, the Philosopher, to go to the Khazars, and his brother took him along to help.
For there were Jews there who were vehemently reviling the Christian faith.
He said, “I am ready to die for the Christian faith,” and did not refuse, but went and served his younger brother like a slave, obeying him.
This one by prayer, and the Philosopher by words, overcame them and put them to shame.
When the emperor and the patriarch saw his good labors on God's path, they urged him to let them consecrate him as archbishop of an honored see where such a man was needed.
When he was unwilling, they pressed him and appointed him abbot of the monastery called Polychron, whose income was twenty and four pounds of gold, and there were more than seventy fathers in it.
In those days Rastislav, the Slavic prince, and Svatopluk sent word from Moravia to Emperor Michael, saying:

“By God's mercy we are well, and many Christian teachers have come among us from the Italians, the Greeks, and the Germans, teaching us in different ways. But we Slavs are simple people, and we have no one to guide us into the truth and explain its meaning.
So, good lord, send us a man who will instruct us in all righteousness.”
Then Emperor Michael said to Constantine the Philosopher:
“Do you hear these words, Philosopher?
No one but you can do this.
Here are many gifts for you. Take your brother Methodius, the abbot, and go.
For you are both from Thessalonica, and all the people of Thessalonica speak Slavonic fluently.”
Then they did not dare refuse either God or the emperor, in accordance with the words of the holy apostle Peter, who said, “Fear God; honor the emperor.”
But when they heard the great [?] charge, they devoted themselves to prayer, together with others who were of the same spirit as they were.
Then God revealed Slavonic letters to the Philosopher. He immediately devised the letters, composed a discourse, and set out on the road to Moravia, taking Methodius with him.
And he once again began humbly and obediently to serve the Philosopher and to teach with him.
After three years had passed, they returned from Moravia, having taught disciples.
When Pope Nicholas heard of such a man, he sent for them, wishing to see them as angels of God. He blessed his teaching, placing the Slavonic Gospel on the altar of the holy apostle Peter.
He also ordained the blessed Methodius to the priesthood.

There were also many other people who taught the Slavonic writings, saying that no language should have letters of its own except Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, according to the inscription that Pilate wrote on the Lord's cross.

The pope called them followers of Pilate and adherents of the three languages, pronounced them accursed, and ordered a certain bishop, who was afflicted with the same disease, to ordain three priests and two readers from among the Slavonic disciples.
After many days, as the Philosopher was approaching judgment, he said to his brother Methodius:
Look, brother, we were a pair yoked together, drawing one furrow, and I am [?] in the forest, having finished my day.
But you love the mountain very much. Do not abandon your teaching for the mountain’s sake, for through it you can more readily be saved.
Then Kocel sent to the pope and asked him to send back Methodius, our blessed teacher.

And the pope said, “Not to you alone, but to all those Slavic lands I send him as a teacher from God and from the holy apostle Peter, the first to occupy this throne and the keeper of the keys to the kingdom of heaven.”
And he sent him, having written this letter:
“Hadrian, bishop and servant of God, to Rastislav, Svatopluk, and Kocel.
Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among people.

For we have heard spiritual things about you, and now we have yearned with longing and prayer for your salvation, how the Lord has stirred your hearts to seek him and shown you that you ought to serve God not only through faith but also through good works.
For faith without works is dead, and those who think they know God but deny him by their works fall away.
For you requested a teacher not only from this episcopal throne, but also from the faithful emperor Michael.
And he sent you the blessed philosopher Constantine together with his brother, before we were able to do so.
But the two of them, learning that your lands belonged to the apostolic see, did nothing contrary to church law, but came to us, bringing the relics of Saint Clement.

And we, receiving threefold joy, decided after examination to send Methodius, having ordained him together with his disciples, our son, to your lands, a man mature in understanding and orthodox in faith, to teach you as you requested, translating the books into your language, fully according to the entire order of the Church, including the holy Mass, that is, the liturgy, and baptism, just as Constantine the philosopher began through God’s grace and the prayers of Saint Clement.

Likewise, if anyone else can translate worthily and in accordance with the true faith, let it be holy and blessed by God, by us, and by the whole catholic and apostolic Church, so that you may readily learn God’s commandments.

But observe this one custom: at Mass, let them first read the Epistle and the Gospel in Latin, and then in Slavonic, so that the word of Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘All nations shall praise the Lord,’ and elsewhere: ‘All shall speak in different tongues of the mighty deeds of God, as the Holy Spirit gives them utterance.’

But if any of the teachers gathered among you, who tickle ears and turn people away from the truth toward falsehoods, should dare to lead you astray in another direction, disparaging the books in your language, let him be excluded not only from [?] but also from the Church until he reforms.
For they are wolves, not sheep, and they ought to be driven out on account of their fruits, and you must guard yourselves against them.
But you, beloved children, obey God’s teaching and do not reject the Church’s instruction, May you be found true worshipers of God our heavenly Father, together with all the saints. Amen.

Kocel also received him with great honor and sent him back to the pope with twenty honorable men from his people, so that the pope might consecrate him as bishop for him in Pannonia, on the throne of the holy apostle Andronicus, one of the Seventy. And this was done.

After this, the ancient enemy, envious of goodness and opposed to truth, stirred up against him the heart of the Moravian king’s enemy, together with all the bishops, who said, “You are teaching in our territory.”
He answered, “If I had known that it was yours, I would have kept away. But it belongs to Saint Peter.

But if, in fact, out of jealousy and greed you encroach upon the ancient boundaries in violation of the canons, hindering God’s teaching, beware lest, in trying to break through an iron mountain with your bony skulls, you spill your brains.”
They said to him angrily, “You will come to harm.”
He answered, “I speak the truth before kings and am not ashamed. Do to me whatever you wish.
For I am no better than those who, for speaking the truth, departed this life amid many torments.”
After many arguments had been directed against him for him to answer, the king said, looking down, “Do not trouble my Methodius. He is already sweating as though beside a furnace.”
He said, “Yes, my lord. Once, some people met a philosopher who was sweating and asked him, ‘Why are you sweating?’ He said, ‘I have been arguing with ignorant people.’”
After quarreling over this remark, they dispersed. They sent him away to Swabia and kept him there for two and a half years.
Word reached the pope, and when he learned of it, he placed them under a ban: none of the king’s bishops were to celebrate Mass, that is, the liturgy, [?] as long as they held him.
And so they released him, saying to Kocel, “If you keep this man with you, you will not escape us unharmed.”
But they did not escape Saint Peter’s judgment, for four of their bishops died.

It happened then that the Moravians discovered that the German priests living among them were not well disposed toward them but were plotting against them. They drove them all out and sent word to the pope:
“Since our fathers formerly received baptism from Saint Peter, give us Methodius as archbishop and teacher.”
The pope immediately sent him.
Prince Svatopluk received him with all the Moravians and entrusted to him all the churches and clergy in every town.
From that day onward, God’s teaching began to spread greatly, the clergy increased in every town, and the pagans began to believe in the true God, renouncing their errors.
All the more did the Moravian realm begin to expand in every direction and defeat its enemies without fail, just as they themselves are continually victorious.
The gift of prophecy was also in him, for many of his predictions came true. We shall recount one or two of them.
A very powerful pagan prince who lived on the Vistula mocked the Christians and did them harm.

Methodius sent word to him, saying, “It would be good for you, son, to be baptized of your own free will in your own land, lest you be taken captive and forcibly baptized in a foreign land. Then you will remember me.” And so it happened.

On another occasion, when Svatopluk was fighting against the pagans and achieving nothing, but only delaying, as Saint Peter’s Mass—that is, the service—was approaching, he sent him a message, saying:
“If you promise to spend Saint Peter’s Day with your troops at my place, I believe in God that he will soon deliver them into your hands.” And so it happened.
Another man, a very wealthy friend and counselor, married his [?], that is, his sister-in-law.
Although he admonished, instructed, and pleaded with them at length, he could not separate the two.
For others, pretending to be servants of God, secretly led them astray, flattering them for the sake of their wealth, so that in the end they were cut off from the Church.
And he said: “The hour will come when these flatterers of yours cannot help you, and you two will remember my words, but there will be nothing you can do.”
Suddenly, when God withdrew his protection, disaster fell upon the two of them, and no place was found for them; it scattered them as a whirlwind takes up and scatters dust.
And there were many other things like these, which he plainly declared in parables.

Unable to endure all this, the ancient enemy, who envies the human race, stirred up certain men against him, as Dathan and Abiram rose against Moses, some openly and others secretly. They are afflicted with the Hyiopatorian heresy and turn the weaker ones away from the right path to themselves, saying:
“The pope has given authority to us, and he orders this man and his teaching to be driven out.”
Having assembled all the people of Moravia, they ordered the letter to be read aloud before them, so that they would hear of his expulsion.

As is natural for human beings, all the people grieved and lamented that they were being deprived of such a shepherd and teacher, except for the weak, whom deceit stirred like the wind stirring leaves.

But when they read the pope’s letter, they found it written: “Our brother Methodius is holy and orthodox, and he does the work of an apostle. All the Slavic lands have been placed in his hands by God and the apostolic see, so let whoever he curses be cursed, and whoever he sanctifies be holy.”
Put to shame, they dispersed like mist, in disgrace.
Their malice did not stop there, however, but they said: “The emperor is angry with him, and if he finds him, he will not be allowed to live.”
But merciful God, unwilling to let his servant be disgraced in this matter either, put a thought into the emperor’s heart—for the emperor’s heart is always in God’s hand—and he sent him a letter:
“Honored father, I greatly desire to see you.
So please do us the kindness of making the journey to us, so that we may see you while you are still in this world and receive your prayer.”
He went there at once, and the emperor received him with great honor and joy. He praised his teaching and retained a priest and a deacon from among his disciples, together with their books.
He fulfilled all his wishes, whatever he wanted, refusing him nothing, and gave him generous gifts before sending him back with honor to his own see. The patriarch did likewise.

On all his journeys he encountered many dangers through the devil’s hostility: robbers in deserted places, wind-driven waves at sea, and sudden deadly perils on rivers, so that the words of the apostle were fulfilled in him:

dangers from robbers, dangers at sea, dangers in rivers, dangers from false brothers, in toil and hardship, often in sleeplessness, often in hunger and thirst, and in the other afflictions that the apostle mentions.

Then, setting aside all disturbances and casting his cares upon God, he first appointed two priests from among his disciples who were very fast scribes, and quickly translated all the books in full, except Maccabees, from Greek into Slavonic in six months, beginning in the month of March and continuing until the twenty-sixth day of October.
When he had finished, he gave due praise and glory to God, who grants such grace and success.
And having offered the holy mystical sacrifice with his clergy, he celebrated the commemoration of Saint Demetrius.
For previously he had translated with the Philosopher only the Psalter, the Gospel, Acts and the Epistles, and selected church services.
Then he also translated the Nomocanon, that is, the rule of law, and the books of the Fathers.
When the king of Hungary came to the regions along the Danube, he wished to see him.
Although some said and supposed that he would not escape him without torture, he went to him.
But the king received him with joy, honor, and glory, as befitted a bishop.

And after conversing with him as it was fitting for two such men to converse, he embraced and kissed him and sent him away with great gifts, saying to him: “Remember me always in your holy prayers, honored father.”
Thus he cut off all grounds for accusation on every side and stopped the mouths of those who spoke at length. He finished his race and kept the faith, awaiting the crown of righteousness.
And because he had thus pleased God, he was beloved.
The time began to draw near for him to receive rest from his sufferings and the reward for his many labors.
They questioned him, saying, “Honored father and teacher, whom among your disciples do you have in mind to succeed you in your teaching?”
He pointed out to them one of his trusted disciples, named Gorazd, saying:
“This is a free man of your own land, well versed in Latin books and orthodox in faith. Let this be God’s will and your love, as it is mine.”
When all the people had gathered on Palm Sunday, he entered the church, though ill, and pronounced a blessing on the emperor, the prince, the clergy, and all the people.
And he said, “Watch over me, children, until the third day.” And so it happened.
As the third day dawned, he finally said, “Into your hands, Lord, I entrust my soul.”
And he fell asleep in the arms of the priests on the sixth day of April, in the third [?]. Indiction [?], in the year 6393 from the creation of the whole world.
His disciples prepared him for burial and paid him due honor. They performed the church service in Latin, Greek, and Slavonic and laid him in the cathedral church.
And he was gathered to his fathers and to the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, teachers, and martyrs.

An innumerable crowd of people gathered and accompanied him with candles, mourning their good teacher and shepherd: men and women, young and old, rich and poor, the free and slaves, widows and orphans, foreigners and local people, the sick and the healthy—all mourning the one who had become all things to all people, so that he might win them all.

But you, O holy and honored head, look down from on high through your prayers upon us who long for you, deliver your disciples from every affliction, spreading the teaching and driving away heresies, so that, having lived here in a manner worthy of your calling, we, your flock, may stand with you at the right hand of Christ our God, receiving eternal life from him.
For to him belong glory and honor forever and ever. Amen.
